2025.clinched: Rally Saudi Arabia, 29 November 2025, the final round
2025.note: Ogier arrived three points behind Elfyn Evans and left with a ninth title, equalling Sébastien Loeb’s record. A Friday puncture wrecked Evans’s rally; Ogier began the last day sixth, one place ahead of him, then charged on the penultimate Asfan stage to third as two rivals stopped for wheels and another rolled. A measured run through the Power Stage settled it, 293 points to 289. He had entered only 11 of the 14 rounds, sitting out Sweden, Kenya and Estonia, won six of them and finished off the podium once. Thierry Neuville won the rally on its first appearance on the calendar.

2024.note: Neuville had been near the front of this championship for a decade before it finally came to him, and it came because Ott Tänak crashed while leading on the last day in Japan. He finished the year on 242 points to Evans’s 210 and Tänak’s 200, from only two rally wins, at Monte Carlo and the Acropolis. It was the first drivers’ title for Hyundai, and Toyota still took the manufacturers’ championship by three points.

2023.clinched: Central European Rally, 2023, the penultimate round
2023.note: Rovanperä finished second on the new event to settle a second consecutive title after his rival and teammate Elfyn Evans crashed out on the Saturday. He ended the season on 250 points to Evans’s 216, with five wins including Portugal, Estonia and the Acropolis. Toyota had already wrapped up the manufacturers’ championship a round earlier at Rally Chile, more than a hundred points clear of Hyundai. Ogier, contesting a partial season, took a ninth Monte Carlo win to pass Loeb’s record at the event.

2022.clinched: Rally New Zealand, 2022, with two rounds to spare
2022.note: Rovanperä became the youngest world rally champion at 22 years and one day, breaking Colin McRae’s record of 27 years and 89 days which had stood since 1995. He won five rallies, in Sweden, Croatia, Portugal, Kenya and Estonia, and finished 50 points clear of Tänak. Toyota took the manufacturers’ title as well.

2021.note: Ogier took an eighth title at Monza, 23 points clear of Elfyn Evans, in what proved the last season alongside Julien Ingrassia, the co-driver he had won all eight with. He opened the year with a record-extending Monte Carlo win and added Croatia by six tenths of a second, Sardinia and Kenya. He had announced he was stopping full-time competition at the end of 2020 and then signed for one more year. Toyota won the manufacturers’ championship by 59 points.

2020.clinched: Rally Monza, December 2020, the final round
2020.note: Only seven rallies were completed, the fewest of any season in the history of the series, after the pandemic wiped out Argentina, Portugal, Kenya, Finland, New Zealand, Germany, Britain, Japan and Belgium. Evans led the championship for most of what was left of it and then went off the road on the icy, slushy deciding stage at Monza, where Ogier won the rally and the title by eight points. It made Ogier and Ingrassia the first crew to win the championship with three different manufacturers. Hyundai took the manufacturers’ title by five points.

2019.clinched: Rally Catalunya, 2019, with an unassailable 36-point lead
2019.note: Tänak became the first Estonian world rally champion and the first driver other than Loeb or Ogier to win the title since 2003, ending fifteen consecutive championships between the two Frenchmen. He won six rallies: Sweden, Chile, Portugal, Sardinia, Finland and Germany. Hyundai took its first manufacturers’ championship in the same season. Rally Australia, which should have closed the year, was cancelled because of the bushfires.

2018.season: thirteen rounds in 2018, and a title won for a team that did not win the manufacturers’ championship
2018.note: Ogier took a sixth consecutive title with M-Sport Ford, 18 points ahead of Neuville, while Toyota won the manufacturers’ championship — its first since 1999 — by 27 points over Hyundai. The fight ran to the closing rounds, with Neuville leading at times and Tänak mounting a late surge of three consecutive victories.

2017.season: thirteen rounds in 2017, the first under the new World Rally Car rules
2017.note: Ogier moved to M-Sport Ford after Volkswagen withdrew in the wake of the emissions scandal, and won a fifth consecutive title there, 32 points clear of Neuville. It was the first drivers’ championship for a privateer team since Ari Vatanen in 1981, and M-Sport took the manufacturers’ title too, its first since 2007. The regulations changed substantially: engine outputs rose from around 300 to 380 bhp and the aerodynamics were opened up. Toyota returned after eighteen years away and Citroën came back with a full factory effort.

2016.clinched: Rally Catalunya, 2016, with one round to spare
2016.note: Ogier’s fourth consecutive title came at the penultimate round, ahead of his Volkswagen teammate Jari-Matti Latvala with Hayden Paddon third. Volkswagen took a fourth straight manufacturers’ championship. Rally China had been cancelled earlier in the year after flooding, and Citroën had already withdrawn factory support to concentrate on the new regulations. Weeks after the season ended Volkswagen announced it was leaving the championship altogether.

2015.clinched: Rally Australia, 2015, with three rounds to spare
2015.note: Ogier won the rally and the title in Australia, the earliest he ever settled one. He had opened the season by winning Monte Carlo, Sweden and Mexico, the Mexico win being his fifth in succession counting the end of the previous year. It was a third consecutive drivers’ and manufacturers’ double for Volkswagen.

2014.clinched: Rally de Catalunya, 2014, with one round to spare
2014.note: Ogier won in Catalunya to take a second title, ahead of his Volkswagen teammate Jari-Matti Latvala with Andreas Mikkelsen third, and Volkswagen defended the manufacturers’ championship. Hyundai returned to the series for the first time since 2003, and Robert Kubica, the former Formula One driver and reigning WRC2 champion, moved up to the top class.

2013.clinched: Rallye de France Alsace, 2013, with two rounds to spare
2013.note: Ogier’s first title ended Loeb’s run of nine consecutive championships, which came to a stop mainly because Loeb chose not to contest a full season and entered only four events. Ogier won it for Volkswagen in the marque’s debut year, and Volkswagen took the manufacturers’ championship as a newcomer too, sealing it at Rally de España. Neuville was runner-up and Latvala third.

2012.note: Loeb’s ninth and last title, a record that stood alone until Ogier matched it in 2025. He opened the season with a sixth Monte Carlo win, then settled the championship in France. Citroën took the manufacturers’ title as well. It was the end of the longest run of dominance the championship has seen: nine drivers’ championships in a row.

2011.note: Loeb secured an eighth consecutive title in Wales after a season with five rally wins, and Citroën took the manufacturers’ championship again. By this point he had won every drivers’ title since 2004.

2010.clinched: Rallye de France, 2010, at home in Haguenau
2010.note: Loeb won a seventh consecutive title on the roads around his home town, having taken seven rally wins across the season. Citroën took the manufacturers’ championship. Rallye de France had moved to Alsace, which is how the clinching event came to be held where he grew up.

2009.note: Loeb won the last rally of the season to take a sixth consecutive title, and Citroën took the manufacturers’ championship. Nobody had won six in the series before him.

2008.note: Loeb became the first five-time world rally champion in Japan, in a season that included a run of five consecutive rally wins. Citroën took the manufacturers’ championship. He had beaten Marcus Grönholm to the title the year before; Grönholm retired at the end of 2007, removing the one rival who had consistently pushed him.

2007.clinched: Wales Rally GB, 2 December 2007, the final round
2007.note: The closest fight of Loeb’s nine titles. Grönholm led him by nine points at the summer break and won Rally New Zealand by three tenths of a second, the narrowest margin in the history of the championship, before crashing in Japan and again in Ireland. Loeb won eight rallies and took the title in Wales at the last event. Ford took the manufacturers’ championship, so the drivers’ and manufacturers’ titles went different ways.

2006.clinched: Rally Australia, 2006, an event Loeb did not start
2006.note: Loeb broke his arm in a mountain-bike accident and missed the end of the season, and the title was settled while he was at home: Grönholm failed to finish in Australia and could no longer catch him. Loeb had built a commanding lead before the injury. Ford took the manufacturers’ championship, and Loeb’s entry that year ran under the Kronos Citroën banner rather than the works team.

2005.note: The most dominant season of Loeb’s career: ten rally wins, a record for a single season, beating the six Didier Auriol managed in 1992. He finished 56 points clear, which broke a 25-year-old record margin of 54 points set by Walter Röhrl in 1980. Citroën took the manufacturers’ championship.

2004.season: sixteen rounds in 2004, and the first of nine consecutive titles
2004.note: Loeb won six rallies and finished 36 points ahead of Petter Solberg, the defending champion, to begin a run that would last until 2012. Citroën took the manufacturers’ championship. Solberg remains the last driver to have beaten Loeb to the title in a straight fight over a full season.

2003.clinched: Wales Rally GB, 9 November 2003, the final round
2003.note: Solberg arrived one point behind Loeb and Carlos Sainz, who were tied on 63, and won the rally to take the championship by a single point. Sainz crashed out on the Trawscoed stage, turning it into a two-man fight; Solberg set the fastest times through the long Rheola and Resolfen stages, took the lead and stayed there, finishing 43.6 seconds ahead of Loeb. He was the first Norwegian world rally champion, and he is still the only driver to have beaten Loeb over a full season. Five different drivers led the championship during the year, and Citroën took the manufacturers’ title.

2002.season: fourteen rounds in 2002, and six rally wins
2002.note: Grönholm took a second title for Peugeot with six victories in the 206 WRC, and Peugeot took the manufacturers’ championship. He was the last champion before Loeb’s nine-year run began.

2001.note: Four drivers could still take the title in Wales, three of them former champions, and the press called it the Battle of Britain because Burns and Colin McRae were the two leading it. McRae won the opening superspecial in Cardiff Bay and was quickest on Friday morning before rolling his Ford out of the rally on the next stage; Tommi Mäkinen also crashed out on the first day. Third place and four points were enough for Burns and his co-driver Robert Reid. He was the first Englishman to win the championship, and Peugeot took the manufacturers’ title. Burns died on 25 November 2005, four years to the day after winning it.

2000.note: Grönholm finished second to Richard Burns in Wales, and second was enough for a first title. He won four rallies that year, in Sweden, New Zealand, Finland and Australia, and Peugeot took the manufacturers’ championship with the 206 WRC.

1999.note: Mäkinen won four rallies and finished on 62 points to complete four championships in a row for Mitsubishi, a run no driver had managed before him. Toyota took the manufacturers’ championship, and would not win another until 2018.

1998.clinched: Rally GB, 1998, the final round, 300 metres from the end
1998.note: Carlos Sainz was leading the championship fight into the last stage of the season and stopped with a mechanical failure roughly 300 metres from the finish, handing Mäkinen a third consecutive title. Mäkinen won five rallies and finished on 58 points, and Mitsubishi took the manufacturers’ championship. It is the closest anyone has come to losing a world title within sight of the line.

1997.note: Mäkinen beat Colin McRae by a single point after the last rally of the year, driving the Mitsubishi Lancer Evo IV, with Sainz third. Subaru took the manufacturers’ championship, so the two titles went different ways. This was the first season under World Rally Car rules, which removed the requirement to mass-produce a road-going version of the car and brought more manufacturers into the sport.

1996.note: Mäkinen built his first title on a controlled Safari Rally win and consolidated it in Australia, finishing the season on 123 points with five rally victories and beating Colin McRae to it. Subaru took the manufacturers’ championship. It was the first of the four consecutive titles he won for Mitsubishi.

1995.note: McRae and Carlos Sainz went to the RAC Rally level on points, and McRae won his home event to take the title. He was the first British world rally champion and, at 27 years and 89 days, the youngest until Kalle Rovanperä in 2022. Subaru took the manufacturers’ championship with the Impreza 555.

1994.note: Auriol became the first French world rally champion when Sainz went off the road on the final day in Britain. He won three rallies that year, in Corsica, Argentina and Sanremo, driving the Toyota Celica Turbo 4WD, and Toyota took the manufacturers’ championship. Two years earlier he had won six rallies in a season, a record that stood until 2005, and had not won the title.

1993.note: Kankkunen won five rallies in the Toyota Celica Turbo 4WD to become the first four-time world rally champion, and Toyota took the manufacturers’ championship. It was his third manufacturer: he had won with Peugeot, then Lancia, and now Toyota, a feat matched only by Ogier in 2020.

1992.note: A three-way fight went to the last rally and Sainz won it, ahead of Ari Vatanen and Juha Kankkunen, to take a second title in the Toyota Celica Turbo 4WD. Kankkunen, his own Toyota teammate, was runner-up. Lancia took the manufacturers’ championship. The season’s most-winning driver was neither of them: Didier Auriol took six rally victories, a record that stood until 2005, and finished behind both.

1991.season: a first third title in 1991, on a record points total
1991.note: Kankkunen finished the season on 150 points, the highest total the championship has recorded, with five rally wins in the Lancia Delta Integrale 16V and Sainz as runner-up. He was the first driver to win three drivers’ titles. Lancia took the manufacturers’ championship.

1990.season: twelve rounds in 1990, and four rally wins
1990.note: Sainz won the Acropolis, New Zealand, the 1000 Lakes and the RAC to take his first title in the Toyota Celica GT-Four, with Didier Auriol runner-up. His 1000 Lakes victory made him the first driver from outside the Nordic countries to win that rally. Lancia took the manufacturers’ championship, so the two titles went different ways.

1989.note: Biasion won five rallies and finished on 106 points in the Lancia Delta HF Integrale 16V, becoming only the second driver to defend the championship after Kankkunen. Lancia took the manufacturers’ title. At his peak he was winning close to three quarters of the events he entered.

1988.season: a first title in 1988, at the start of the Lancia Delta’s dominance
1988.note: Biasion won five rallies and finished on 115 points in the Lancia Delta HF Integrale, and Lancia took the manufacturers’ championship. The Delta had arrived when Group B was banned and the championship moved to production-based Group A cars, and it went on to win more than any rally car before or since.

1987.season: a second title in 1987, and the first successful defence
1987.note: Kankkunen moved from Peugeot to Lancia for the first Group A season and became the first driver to defend the world championship, winning the Olympus Rally and the RAC among others in the Delta HF 4WD. Lancia took the manufacturers’ title, and his own teammates Miki Biasion and Markku Alén were next in the standings.

1986.season: a title in 1986 that changed hands eleven days after the season ended
1986.note: Kankkunen won three rallies in the Peugeot 205 Turbo 16 E2 with Markku Alén second, in a season cut short in every sense: Group B was banned after Henri Toivonen and Sergio Cresto were killed on the Tour de Corse. Peugeot was then excluded from the Rallye Sanremo on a technicality, which briefly handed the championship to Alén, and the appeal that reversed it succeeded eleven days after the final round. Kankkunen became the youngest champion in the history of the series, and Peugeot took the manufacturers’ title.

1985.season: twelve rounds in 1985, and five rally wins
1985.note: Salonen beat the Audis of Stig Blomqvist and Walter Röhrl to the title in the Peugeot 205 Turbo 16, winning in Portugal, Greece, New Zealand, Argentina and Finland, and Peugeot took its first manufacturers’ championship ahead of Audi and Lancia. The season also brought the death of Attilio Bettega on the Tour de Corse in May, one of the accidents that would end Group B.

1984.season: twelve rounds in 1984, and Audi at its peak
1984.note: Blomqvist won five rallies to take the title ahead of his Audi teammate Hannu Mikkola, with Markku Alén third, and Audi took the manufacturers’ championship. The Quattro A2 won six of the first eight events and swept the podium at the first two. The warning came late: Ari Vatanen debuted Peugeot’s 205 Turbo 16 and won three of the last four rallies.

1983.season: twelve rounds in 1983, decided between two cars
1983.note: Mikkola took the drivers’ title with four wins and seven podiums in the Audi Quattro, the first world rally champion in a four-wheel-drive car, with Walter Röhrl and Markku Alén his closest rivals. Audi and Lancia between them won ten of the twelve events and filled 30 of the 36 podium places. Lancia took the manufacturers’ championship by two points, having withdrawn from the final two rounds while Audi won three of the last four.

1982.season: a second title in 1982, in a rear-wheel-drive car
1982.note: Röhrl won three rallies and finished on 109 points in the Opel Ascona 400, holding off the four-wheel-drive Audis in a car whose layout was already obsolete. The runner-up was Michèle Mouton, the closest a woman has come to winning the championship, and Audi took the manufacturers’ title. His two championships came with two different manufacturers.

1981.clinched: the 1981 season, won by a privateer entry
1981.note: Vatanen finished on 96 points to Guy Fréquelin’s 89, with Hannu Mikkola third, after winning in Greece, Argentina, Brazil and Finland in a Ford Escort RS1800 run by the Rothmans Rally Team. It is the only time a privateer team won the drivers’ championship until Ogier and M-Sport in 2017. Talbot took the makes’ championship with the Sunbeam Lotus, so no manufacturer team won the drivers’ title at all.

1980.season: a first title in 1980, by the largest margin then recorded
1980.note: Röhrl won four rallies and finished on 118 points in the Fiat 131 Abarth, with Ari Vatanen runner-up, and Fiat took the manufacturers’ championship. His winning margin of 54 points stood as the record for 25 years, until Loeb beat it by two in 2005.

1979.season: the first World Rally Championship for Drivers, in 1979, decided by one point
1979.note: Waldegård finished on 112 points to Hannu Mikkola’s 111 in the closest possible start to the drivers’ championship, with Markku Alén third on 68. He won four rallies, the Acropolis, New Zealand, the Critérium du Québec and the RAC, in a Ford Escort RS1800, and Ford took its first manufacturers’ championship on 122 points ahead of Datsun and Fiat. Two later championships were settled by the same single point, in 1997 and 2003.
